title: The 10 Best Corded Impact Wrenches
subtitle: Wired impact wrenches ranked from live Amazon data — the corded impact tool for lug nuts and bolts.
intro: Quick note on names: there is no such thing as a corded impact driver — the impact-driver format (1/4-inch hex, for screws) is inherently cordless. The corded impact tool that actually exists is the impact wrench: a 1/2-inch square drive that spins sockets to break loose and tighten lug nuts, suspension bolts, and rusted hardware. This list covers electric corded impact wrenches — the ones that plug into a wall outlet (120V) or a car's 12V socket. If you want to drive screws, you want an impact driver from the cordless list; if you want to wrench on a car without an air compressor, you're in the right place.
data_source: Amazon product listings on the data_captured date. Prices, ratings and review counts change daily; check the listing before relying on a number.

products.name: CRAFTSMAN CMEF901 7.5-Amp 1/2" Corded Impact Wrench (450 ft-lbs)

cons: About three times the price of the Eastvolt
8.7 lb, heavy for overhead work

avoid.name: Ingersoll Rand 231C 1/2" Air Impact Wrench
avoid.flag: Excellent tool — but it's pneumatic and needs an air compressor
avoid.verdict: To be clear, this is a superb impact wrench and a shop standard. The catch: it's pneumatic. It doesn't plug into a wall outlet; it needs a good-sized air compressor to run. Buy it only if you already have one.
reasons: It runs on compressed air, not electricity. There's no plug — you need an air compressor (realistically a $200+ pancake or larger) and a hose to use it at all.
A small hobby compressor can't keep up with it; it wants real CFM, so the true cost is the wrench plus a capable compressor.
If you want to plug into a wall outlet and go, buy the CRAFTSMAN or Eastvolt above instead. They're corded-electric, no air needed.
It's on this 'avoid' list only because it's the wrong category for someone shopping electric impact wrenches — in a shop with air, it's a great buy.

buyers_guide.a: An impact driver has a 1/4-inch hex chuck for driving screws and small fasteners — and it's a cordless-only format. An impact wrench has a 1/2-inch (or 3/8") square drive that spins sockets to loosen and tighten bolts and lug nuts. If you want to drive screws, see the cordless impact drivers.

AC corded wrenches plug into a wall outlet for shop-grade power. 12V wrenches run off a car socket for roadside tire changes — handy but light-duty. Air (pneumatic) wrenches are powerful but need an air compressor. This list focuses on the electric ones you can plug in.

A corded electric impact wrench gives sustained power for less money than a comparable cordless model, and never runs out of charge — good for a home garage with an outlet. Cordless wins only if you need to work far from power.

buyers_guide.q: How much torque do I need?
buyers_guide.a: For car lug nuts (usually 80-100 ft-lbs to spec, more when rusted or over-torqued), aim for a wrench rated around 300-450 ft-lbs of breakaway so it actually cracks them loose. The 12V roadside tools sit well below that — fine for a spare, not for stuck bolts.

It's a socket retainer that lets you push sockets on and pull them off by hand — fast and convenient. A detent-pin anvil holds sockets more securely but is slower to change. For general use, a hog ring is the friendlier choice.
